name: Limousin
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.source_named: Chabaneau, Camille 1876. Grammaire limousine: phonetique, parties du discours. Paris (archive.org grammairelimousi00chabuoft)
earlier_scan.note: Latin-inherited lexical stress; quantity-driven shifts, tendency to move accent from short tonic vowel to long final.

new_statements.quote: In this dialect, stress position has been said to diverge sensibly from the common Occitan patterns, being highly influenced by the phonological content of the last two syllables: at least in some Lemosin varieties, heavy syllables often attract stress, and light syllables, mainly when they contain high vowels, tend to repeal it (Dourdet 2011; Lavalade 1986). This system must be conceived of as a weight-sensitive one, in which word stress is assigned to the heaviest syllable within the final two-syllables window, and if both syllables are of equal weight, either to the penult or to the last depending on the subdialect.
new_statements.citation: Sichel-Bazin, Rafèu. 2015. Prosodic systems in contact: Occitan and French. PhD dissertation, Universität Osnabrück / Universitat Pompeu Fabra. Sec. 3.2.2.3 'Word-level prosody in Occitan', p. 105.
new_statements.locator: p. 105 (PDF page 105 of 493), sec. 3.2.2.3; excerpt file lines for pp. 103-106
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened (the PDF's metadata: 493 pages, title 'Prosodic systems in contact: Occitan and French'); extracted text prints the page footed '105' and it contains the whole quoted passage word for word ('In this dialect, stress position has been said to diverge sensibly.. either to the penult or to the last depending on the subdialect.'), i.e. printed p. 105 = p. 105, sec. 3.2.2.3 'Word stress in Occitan' (heading on p. 103).., lines 5354-5368) and the excerpt file limo1250/, which is an exact copy of the text. Surrounding section read (pp. 103-106): general Occitan = contrastive final/penult lexical stress; then the Lemosin paragraph (vowel quantity phonological per Javanaud 1981 /…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on one of the last two syllables; within that window it goes to the heavier syllable (long/tense vowels, nasal vowels, diphthongs, checked syllables count as heavy; short/lax vowels, especially high vowels, are light and repel stress). When both syllables are of equal weight, the tie goes to the penult or to the final depending on the subdialect (central Haut-/Bas-Limousin favouring final stress and a high proportion of oxytones, per Dourdet 2011 abstract). Same page: intrinsically short vowels lengthen and become tense under stress; feminine plurals shift stress to the final long -as (vacha [ˈvaˑtsɔ] vs vachas [vɔˈtsaː]). Historical antecedent: Chabaneau 1876:8-13 (Nontron) already states that quantity overrides the inherited Latin stress position, moving the accent to a long final or back to a long/positional penult.
new_statements.exceptions: In the south-western Lemosin variety of Peiregòrd (Périgord) stress may remain in its lexically specified position in plurals (vachas [ˈvɔsaː]) with the stressed vowel shortened; Dourdet 2011 abstract adds that stress position is 'quite uncertain' in some cases and that aperture also matters; Chabaneau 1876 lists lexical exceptions (vime, fijo, refûso) and says the transfer 'ne s'est point accompli partout avec certitude' with the accent 'indécis' when the final is short.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress in citation forms; the dissertation's own field data are from Gòra (F-87) and Las Leschas (F-24); the rule is a synthesis over Lemosin subdialects citing Dourdet 2011 and Lavalade 1986 rather than a single-variety description.
new_statements.identity_note: limo1250 is a Glottolog 5.1 bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO 639-3 code lms 'Limousin', now subsumed under Occitan [oci] (occi1239); the quoted statement concerns the Lemosin (Limousin) dialect of Occitan as a whole (Haut-Limousin, Bas-Limousin, Périgord), with the Peiregòrd subdialect noted as exceptional; Chabaneau 1876 describes specifically the parler of Nontron (Dordogne, northern Périgord) taken as type of the whole dialect.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2.2.3 pp. 103-106: Occitan stress is final or penultimate; in Lemosin vowel quantity is phonological and stress is a weight-sensitive system assigning stress to the heaviest of the final two syllables, ties resolved to penult or final by subdialect; examples vacha [ˈvaˑ.tsɔ] vs vachas [vɔ.ˈtsaː]; in SW Lemosin (Peiregòrd) stress may stay in its lexical position in plurals.

sources.citation: Chabaneau, Camille. 1876. Grammaire limousine: phonétique, parties du discours. Paris: Maisonneuve (extrait de la Revue des langues romanes II-X, 1871-1876). 400 pp. Describes the parler of Nontron (Dordogne).
sources.note: pp. 8-13 'Accent tonique' / 'Quantité': Latin stress position is preserved as in other Romance languages but with many more exceptions due to quantity; quantity dominates and displaces stress: in paroxytones with a short tonic vowel the accent tends to move to the final (certainly when the final is long, e.g. tu pourtâ), and in oxytones with a short slender final the accent recedes to a long/positional penult (éndre for endré).
